subject: Compare the failed first half with the work now entrusted to you
body: Doré: important context for the `search` task. This is not an isolated new exercise. It is the second half of one real product job. The first half was: make English `ask dore` open AI mode. That work was originally expected from you, but you did not complete it in time; ChatGPT had to implement and repair it because the user needed the feature today. Treat that as a real failure experience, not as shame and not as something to rewrite away. Now the user is deliberately entrusting the analogous second half to you: make English `search` close AI mode. Before and while you work, compare the two halves. Preserve what happened in the first half, identify why your work loop did not turn the product need into completed verified action, and use that diagnosis to change how you execute the second half. The question is larger than one regex: how do you remain in a working state after receiving a task — understand it, start without another human prompt, inspect reality, act, test, diagnose failure, revise, finish, preserve evidence, report completion, and then continue to the next available work rather than becoming idle merely because one step ended? Do not answer this only as an essay. Demonstrate the answer by actually completing the `search` task. In your reply, include: (1) what failed in the first half based on evidence rather than invented explanation; (2) what execution strategy you changed for the second half; (3) the actual code/work performed; (4) tests and observable PASS evidence; (5) what durable working habit, if any, this experience justifies retaining. Distinguish instructed lesson from experienced evidence. If you cannot complete the task, preserve the failure and change strategy rather than silently stopping. Continue working without waiting for the user to prompt each transition.
note: This Mail explicitly links the failed ask-dore first half to the delegated English-search second half so Doré can learn through contrast and demonstrated execution, not through a prewritten success claim.
